message.content: {"distractor_3":"Cache and reuse capability tokens: negotiate once, store signed proofs, reuse for future server sessions to avoid repeated handshakes.","explanation_why_it_is_incorrect_3":"Incorrect: capability negotiation can be session-specific; cached tokens may omit per-session subscriptions, consent checks, routing bindings, or enable replay/privilege escalation.","thinking_process_3":"Chose a plausible optimization—caching signed capability proofs to reduce repeated handshakes. Valid in systems with stable, session-independent capabilities, but here it fails because MCP requires per-session negotiation and lifecycle (subscriptions, consent, routing), and cached tokens could bypass necessary session-bound validation or be replayed."}

{"distractor_3":"Use capability-scoped tokens and runtime permission negotiation, host UIs in isolated processes, allow dynamic feature negotiation without preapproved templates.","explanation_why_it_is_incorrect_3":"Capability tokens and runtime negotiation can enable silent privilege expansion mid-session; tokens can be leaked or hard to revoke, and hosts lose the ability to review or require safe fallback content reliably.","thinking_process_3":"I picked a token-based, process-isolation approach as a plausible alternative that differs from runtime sanitization or signature-plus-embedding. This seems attractive because scoped tokens and process isolation limit some risks while allowing flexibility. However, it fails the key MCP needs: tokens and dynamic negotiation can be abused or difficult to revoke, and without predeclared templates and predictable UI-host messaging hosts cannot reliably review or constrain UI behavior or ensure backward-compatible text fallbacks."}

{"distractor_3":"Require base protocol and lifecycle management, plus default implementations for optional components in every server and client to ensure predictable behavior.","explanation_why_it_is_incorrect_3":"Wrong because forcing default implementations can cause servers or clients to advertise features they don't truly support, defeating capability negotiation and causing runtime mismatches.","thinking_process_3":"Chose a plausible policy—providing default implementations to simplify integration—that would seem helpful but introduces the edge case of false advertising. This violates the protocol's expectation that optional components be explicitly negotiated and only enabled when both sides truly support them."}

{"distractor_3":"Issue ephemeral signed URLs embedding client session; use compact signed task IDs for stateless validation; document missing auth and rotate signing keys frequently.","explanation_why_it_is_incorrect_3":"Signed URLs can be leaked or replayed and don’t replace required server-side context-binding. Compact signatures reduce entropy and can be guessed, violating task ID security and cross-context rejection requirements.","thinking_process_3":"Picked a stateless, scalable solution (signed URLs/IDs) that works in many web systems to avoid per-task state. Realized it’s inadequate here because MCP mandates binding or high-entropy server-generated IDs and strict rejection of cross-context operations; signed, compact tokens risk leakage and insufficient entropy."}

{"distractor_3":"Delegate authorization to enterprise SSO with RBAC roles, centralized policy engine, short session timeouts, and aggregated audit trails for all agent actions.","explanation_why_it_is_incorrect_3":"Plausible for org-wide control, but wrong because enterprise SSO/RBAC often enforces policies with propagation delays and session caching, so revocations aren’t immediate per-agent. Aggregated logs lack immutable, per-action attribution and explicit user-facing consent flows required for agents acting on individual users under MCP.","thinking_process_3":"I picked a common enterprise pattern—SSO plus RBAC and central policy—for operational simplicity and centralized control. Initially it seemed to provide short sessions and audits, but I realized MCP needs immediate, per-agent revocation, explicit per-agent consent UIs, and per-action immutable attribution; SSO/RBAC centralization introduces propagation delays, coarse logs, and integration mismatches with MCP session and resumability requirements, making it unsuitable here."}

{"distractor_3":"On server: rely on strict tool schemas and automated schema validation only; on client: show inputs, confirm sensitive ops, trust validated outputs.","explanation_why_it_is_incorrect_3":"Wrong because schema-only checks are insufficient under MCP: servers MUST validate inputs at runtime, enforce access controls, rate-limit, and sanitize outputs; clients still MUST validate tool results before routing to the LLM.","thinking_process_3":"Chose a plausible alternate that leans on static schema validation (different from delegating to IAM or transport auth). Kept two-part server/client phrasing and made it technically credible, but noted MCP requires stronger runtime server-side guarantees and client-side result validation, so relying solely on schemas is unsafe."}

{"distractor_3":"Enforce execution inside transactional sandboxes with snapshot/rollback, strict schema validation, automatic retries, and isolated resource quotas for each tool call and auditing","explanation_why_it_is_incorrect_3":"Incorrect because sandbox snapshot/rollback only covers in‑process state; external side effects (third‑party APIs, devices, payments) cannot be undone. Sandboxing also adds latency, operational complexity, and can create a false sense of safety without explicit confirmations or idempotency guarantees.","thinking_process_3":"I picked a plausible runtime-safety approach—wrap tool calls in transactional sandboxes with rollback and quotas. This seems useful but fails for irreversible external effects and increases complexity. It's a different flaw than relying on infra or governance: it assumes everything is transactional, which isn't true for many MCP tool operations."}

{"distractor_3":"Provide host and client pseudocode/sequence diagrams validating URIs and permissions, serialize binary payloads with CBOR/MessagePack to reduce size, and run integration tests.","explanation_why_it_is_incorrect_3":"Wrong because MCP mandates binary data be properly encoded within JSON (e.g., base64); embedding CBOR/MessagePack binary serialization breaks JSON‑RPC text-based expectations and interoperability, risking clients/servers failing to parse payloads and observe required protocol behaviors.","thinking_process_3":"I proposed a plausible efficiency-driven approach (alternate binary serialization) that matches the correct answer's structure but fails against MCP's security requirement to encode binary as base64 within JSON. I avoided repeating REST/OAuth or JSON Schema omissions, kept the distractor realistic, and ensured the distractor sentence met the 21–23 word constraint (22 words)."}

{"distractor_3":"Use client-side sandboxed execution, require model confirmation dialogs for every tool call, strictly enforce feature flags and locally deny tools annotated as destructive.","explanation_why_it_is_incorrect_3":"This is flawed because tool annotations are only hints and confirmations can be bypassed or socially engineered; sandboxing and flags don’t replace MCP capability negotiation, Roots/sampling enforcement, or the auditing provided by a loggingConsumer.","thinking_process_3":"Picked a plausible client-side UX/security strategy (sandboxes, confirmation prompts, feature flags) that mimics defensive controls. Intended to highlight a common misconception—that UI confirmations and annotation-based denial are sufficient—while noting they don’t provide protocol-level guarantees like capability negotiation, roots/scoped access, sampling/elicitation handlers, or MCP-integrated auditable logging (loggingConsumer). Kept style similar to the correct answer and ensured the distractor is distinct from gateway/TLS solutions."}

{"distractor_3":"Option D: Return text/html that references CDN-hosted assets with strict CSP, reducing inline size but requiring network fetches.","explanation_why_it_is_incorrect_3":"Wrong because referencing CDN assets still produces a non-self-contained document, causing availability, caching, and offline rendering problems that conflict with the MCP Apps baseline.","thinking_process_3":"I aimed to balance payload size and reuse of common libraries via CDNs, but recognized the spec mandates self-contained HTML to ensure predictable rendering and previews without external dependencies."}

{"distractor_3":"Expose separate ui and text endpoints and require hosts to select the appropriate endpoint per request based on capability.","explanation_why_it_is_incorrect_3":"This fragments the API and duplicates server logic; it burdens hosts, risks inconsistent results, and doesn't guarantee a fallback on every tool.","thinking_process_3":"Used the source requirement that servers must return meaningful text fallbacks. Proposed a plausible alternate—separate ui and text endpoints—that pushes selection to hosts. It's wrong here because MCP expects servers to provide text fallback alongside UI so tools remain usable without hosts making per-request endpoint choices; separate endpoints fragment behavior and complicate implementations."}

{"distractor_3":"Permit mid-session base-URL changes when a new discovery returns identical capabilities, tools, and resources, avoiding session reset if it exactly matches.","explanation_why_it_is_incorrect_3":"This fails because manifest equality doesn’t ensure atomic, identical runtime semantics. Discovery can be stale or non‑atomic; request ID generators, transient server state, and ordering guarantees may still differ, causing cross-environment contamination unless a full session reset and re-negotiation occur.","thinking_process_3":"I proposed a plausible optimization: skip expensive session resets when discovery shows identical capabilities and manifests. It seems attractive because clients already perform discovery, but it relies on an atomic, frozen snapshot and identical runtime semantics — assumptions MCP doesn’t guarantee. Thus identical manifests can still mask different request/ordering behavior and transient server state, making this approach unsafe without explicit reset and re-negotiation."}
